newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-SELES ADVANCES BUT YEARNS FOR MISSING ZIP ON HER SERVE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SELES ADVANCES BUT YEARNS FOR MISSING ZIP ON HER SERVE.

text.p: Monica Seles yearns to become a 90s woman again.

Seles advanced to another U.S. Open final with a 6-4 6-3 victory Friday over Conchita Martinez, but there was something missing from the killer reportoire she usually brings to battle -- a big 90 mph (145 kph) first serve.
Nursing a shoulder injury that has held her back this year, Seles, 22, consistently served in the 70 mile-per-hour (113 kph) range against the fourth-seeded Spaniard.
"I need to get back in the 90s," said Seles. "I need my 90 serves to play against the top players and have an easier chance of holding my serve against somebody like Steffi (Graf)."
Seles, who lost to Graf in three tense sets in last year's final, meets the winner of the Graf-Martina Hingis semifinal.
Seles, seeded second behind Graf, said she was content to lob in first serves against Martinez.
"She was standing so far back, I didn't want to go that much for too big of a serve because I knew I was not going to ace her," Seles reasoned.
"She was returning (big-serving) Brenda Schultz from back there. As long as she was standing there, I was just going to throw in my first serve and play conservatively."
Seles found the mark with 80 percent of her first serves against 1994 Wimbledon champion Martinez, but the Yugoslav-born American is not so confident about serving in the final.
The co-world number one has never played Hingis, but she knows what she will be up against should she encounter Graf on championship Sunday.
"I will try to make up for it in the groundstrokes," Seles said about her service-power shortage.
"But Steffi has a huge advantage because she has a very high percentage of first serves in the 95s (153 kph). That is a big advantage and that is the one that I am going to try to work towards.

"That is what I tried to do last winter and maybe I was pushing it a little bit too soon after not doing anything with it for 2-1/2 years," she said, referring to her layoff after being stabbed in the back during a match in Hamburg.
"But after my shoulder is back (in shape), I am going to try to do that."
Seles started the Grand Slam season with a bang by winning her fourth Australian Open title and running her career record in Melbourne to an astonishing 28-0.
Then came the shoulder worries that led to a quarter-finals loss at the French Open and a second-round ouster at Wimbledon.
Seles is unsure whether doctors will recommend rest or surgery for her ailing shoulder, but she is determined to get back her 90s persona.
"You see some people who are 5-feet-4 (1.62 m) serving 102s (164 kph). At 5-feet-10 (1.78 m), I should be able to serve 95s on average."
Service speed aside, Seles is eager for another sampling of the sublime pressure of a Grand Slam final.
"I love the matches that are close because as a player that is one of the things you work hard for. When it comes down to close matches, a couple of points will decide it and you love that.
"That is the excitement. That is the rush."
